name: Ivan Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no employer, party or AI company ties. This is confidential. Ivan, what is a normal shift for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: At breakfast I search the fault archive with AI, then I check the original record at the depot and load the fittings. The work is climbing, isolating and repairing lines; I like solving the awkward faults that look easy on a map. I do not like returning because a drawing missed what was buried under a verge.

say: I would say **AI search** can find useful fault records without replacing line repairs.
I would remind the crew a **live joint** still needs careful physical work.
think: I enjoy new tools, but our **thin savings** leave the mortgage exposed to ordinary repairs.
A quiet AI future still leaves **boiler risk** for the household.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** and check AI search results against signed records.
Put **thirty per wage** into a boiler and car account next payday.
feel: I feel **good at work** and uneasy about our cash balance.
S0.quote: We have been lucky with the heating this year, which is not the same as being prepared.
fieldNote: Ivan uses **AI daily** to search fault archives, and a footbridge joint gave him a recent reason to trust verified results.
His new **repair account** responds to thin savings after a car service consumed the family buffer.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts and verify AI fault searches against signed records
Use AI daily to search the company fault archive before repairs
Transfer thirty from each wage into a boiler and car account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the AI search I use at breakfast still helps find old fault notes, even if the technology stops there. A live joint does not care how quickly a screen finds a drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like trying tools, but I cannot pretend the mortgage is light. We have two children in school and less than a month saved, so a quiet technology future still leaves us one broken boiler from borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid line shifts and continue using AI to search the company fault archive, checking its answer against the signed job record. Starting next payday, I would put thirty from each wage into a boiler and car account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel good about the work and uneasy about the bank balance. We have been lucky with the heating this year, which is not the same as being prepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did your AI search last help on a repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Tuesday it found a note about a buried joint near the footbridge. I checked the original record and we dug in the right place instead of opening the whole verge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a separate boiler and car account?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car service took our last spare money in June. A named account would remind us the next repair is predictable even when its date is not.

say: I would support an **AI plan** only if crews can reject errors on site.
I would ask for a **wrong-order record** before a pilot becomes the normal system.
think: A **smaller office** could push more jobs and tighter targets onto the same crew.
I need **paid correction time** because our household relies on the full wage.
do: Volunteer for the paid **planning pilot** and compare fittings at each site.
Send a **monthly error sheet** and teach the next crew from actual mistakes.
feel: I feel **excited by testing** and worried about tighter work targets.
S1.quote: The crew could see how a neat schedule still left us with the wrong metal.
fieldNote: Ivan wants **early pilot access** and learns through site comparisons, matching his daily use of AI.
He connects **minutes on a dashboard** to possible overtime loss and would seek paid correction terms before rollout.

steps.text: Test the paid AI planning pilot against actual site fittings
Ask the union representative to agree paid correction time if rollout proceeds
Continue paid line repairs while testing the pilot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot I would test an AI plan if the crew can still reject a bad one at the pole. The ordering system could save a van trip, but it needs a record of what it gets wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, buying and scheduling can be automated before anyone replaces our hands in the field. I worry that a smaller office will send more jobs per crew, and our overtime may become a target on a dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would volunteer for the first paid planning pilot, compare its suggested fittings with the cupboard on site and teach the next crew what fails. In the first year I would send a monthly error sheet to the supervisor and ask for paid time to correct the orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel excited by the puzzle and worried about how managers count minutes. I have a mortgage, so a clever tool is only a win for me if the wage does not shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach from the first error sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the Oak Lane job where the plan ordered a standard clamp for a corroded bracket. The crew could see how a neat schedule still left us with the wrong metal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a formal agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pilot became the normal system, I would ask the union representative and supervisor to agree on paid correction time. I would not wait until errors were treated as a crew failure.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from field robots around 2031.
I would ask for **human inspection** of first robot repairs in bad weather.
think: I will be **48** at the robot date and have few nearby line options.
Knowing AI prompts does not **protect my wage** if machines do the physical repair.
do: Seek a funded **commissioning course** linked to an advertised field post.
Keep paid **line shifts** after 2028 and save two overtime payments for mortgage cover.
feel: I feel **keyed up**, with time to act but no guarantee.
S2.quote: I would not call myself safe just because I know how to prompt a computer.
fieldNote: Ivan channels his **technology curiosity** into a possible robot commissioning role, but distinguishes field testing from report writing.
The plan is **income constrained**: paid training, comparable pay and two overtime payments for mortgage cover.

steps.text: Keep paid line repair shifts through the first 2028 AI year
Take a funded robot commissioning course if linked to an advertised post
Apply for a comparable field commissioning vacancy if available
Save the next two overtime payments for mortgage cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full AI in 2028 may plan a whole repair, but a robot able to do the line work arrives nearer 2031. I would want the first robot repairs inspected by people who have done the job in bad weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 for the thinking system and 48 for the robot. I am comfortable learning software, yet there are few line vacancies nearby and our savings would disappear in a month if my pay stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the company about paid robot commissioning work and take a funded course if it leads to an advertised post. In the first year after 2028 I would keep the line shifts, apply for a field commissioning vacancy at comparable pay and save the next two overtime payments for mortgage cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel keyed up rather than frozen. The three years of physical work could buy us time, but I would not call myself safe just because I know how to prompt a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would commissioning mean in your hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check whether the robot can isolate a line and fit the right part, then record where a human crew had to take over. If the role only writes reports, full AI could do that part instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner say about the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would ask whether the course hours are paid before talking about anything else. I would agree, because our family cannot cover an unpaid month.

say: I would request **wet-fault trials** before robot repairs are trusted.
I would explain **2031 AI** reaches planning before line robots around 2034.
think: At **51**, I may still owe the mortgage and need paid hours.
A **trial job** might end, so I need regular field duties rather than a temporary title.
do: Join a paid **field trials team** and log human repairs.
In **2031**, keep line shifts and take a funded safety course before applying for a regular trials job.
feel: I feel **more patient** with five years to watch the evidence.
S3.quote: A clean robot-repair trial success rate would fool me without the weather, fitting details and time spent correcting problems.
fieldNote: Ivan asks for **specific trial data** because he expects performance to vary with weather, fittings and isolation steps.
He avoids **pure planning work** after full AI and seeks regular paid field hours before changing jobs.

steps.text: Keep paid line shifts through the first 2031 AI year
Finish a funded company safety course if offered for field trials
Apply for a regular paid field trials job if one opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew five years is enough to keep a proper trial log. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, while robots that can do line work come around 2034; the company should test them against wet, awkward faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 in 2031 and 51 in 2034. My older child might be leaving school, but I may still pay the mortgage and I will not assume a robot test job lasts forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask to join a paid field trials team and record which repairs still need a person. In 2031 I would keep paid line shifts, finish the company safety course if funded, and apply for the trials job only if it has regular hours and a field component.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more patient than in the two-year version. I can watch the equipment improve and decide when a real vacancy is worth moving for, rather than calling every demonstration a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the trial log need besides failures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It needs the weather, the exact fitting, the isolation steps and how long the human crew took to correct a problem. A clean robot-repair trial success rate would fool me without the weather, fitting details and time spent correcting problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you also take a desk planning role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not move into pure planning when full thinking AI could do the schedules. I would stay with field testing or repairs where a real person still has a paid task.

say: I would ask for **yearly pilot evidence** on faults and field hours.
I would note **2036 office AI** precedes line-capable robots around 2039.
think: At **56**, I cannot assume a pension or a paid-off mortgage.
Even a **field testing team** might shrink once robots become capable.
do: Keep paid **line repairs** and track yearly robot faults.
After **2036**, apply for a funded testing vacancy and transfer thirty per wage toward mortgage principal.
feel: I feel **steady now** and realistic about later field job changes.
S4.quote: The gear belongs to the company, while the mortgage belongs to us.
fieldNote: Ivan treats the decade as a chance for **measured experiments** while continuing paid physical work.
His **mortgage payments** remain central; he will not assume a lasting testing team or automatic retirement at 56.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs through the first 2036 AI year
Apply for a funded regular field testing vacancy if available
Transfer thirty from each wage toward mortgage principal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that a decade lets us collect evidence from every robot pilot instead of buying a promise. Full AI in 2036 changes the office first; line-capable robots come around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 for the thinking change and 56 when robots arrive. The children will likely be adults, but the mortgage might still be there, and I have not earned a retirement promise from anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the repair job and ask for yearly figures on field hours and robot faults. In 2036 I would compare those figures with my partner, apply for a funded field testing opening if it had regular pay, and continue transferring thirty from each wage toward the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady about earning for the next few years. The longer warning lets me test a new role while I still have a wage, though I know a field testing team could also shrink after 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep paying the mortgage rather than buy new gear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gear belongs to the company, while the mortgage belongs to us. If I put a little away each wage, a poor overtime month is less frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the field testing opening never appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on paid line repairs while they are available and use the crew-hour figures to judge when to apply elsewhere. I would not set a retirement date from a robot timetable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The field robots would follow around 2031, and our family has too little saved for a wage gap. Paid commissioning training tied to a regular field vacancy, plus honest pilot records, would help me decide without abandoning a paying shift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays when a robot pilot fails and our crew takes over. If trial figures hide the human crew's work after a robot fails, we will lose hours on paper before machines can replace us.

headlineQuote: If trial figures hide the human crew's work after a robot fails, we will lose hours on paper before machines can replace us.
portrait: Ivan is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
He uses **AI daily** to search faults, then checks the original signed record before repairs.
His **thin savings** push him to preserve paid shifts while considering technology roles.
Across the scenarios he seeks **field trial evidence**, funded courses and regular commissioning or testing work rather than pure planning.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** gives him only about three years before robots could do physical line repairs.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **commissioning training**, a regular field vacancy and honest robot trial records would let him move while earning.
